In MACT proceedings, delay in lodging FIR is not fatal when medical exigency intervenes and the accident is otherwise supported by medical and criminal record.
Mere delay, by itself, does not discredit the claimant.
(g) PW-1 admitted that he himself did not possess a driving licence.
However, he was not driving the motorcycle and was only a pillion rider.
Even otherwise, absence of driving licence on the part of victim is not determinative of negligence unless causal connection is established, which is absent in the present case.
(h) Objection was raised as there is no mention of road traffic accident on MLC.
The subsequent medical record clearly mentions road traffic accident and therefore this objection is without merit.

(i) Minor lapses such as inability to recall motorcycle number, non-seizure of motorcycle or absence of street lighting are peripheral circumstances and do not strike at the core issue, particularly when PW-1 consistently maintained that the offending vehicle struck from behind.
Non-examination of Janmajay is also not fatal, as the injured himself has testified and his version is corroborated by criminal record.
Significantly, during cross-examination by the insurance company, no specific challenge was put to PW-1 regarding rash or negligent driving.

(j) It is also relevant that when a stationary or slow-moving vehicle is hit from behind, primary responsibility lies upon the vehicle coming from the rear, which is expected to maintain safe distance and proper control.
The respondents have not led any evidence to rebut this presumption.

Whether the claimant is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom?OPP 9. Sec. 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunals to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable.
Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:

"(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application for compensation made under section 166, the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be,
each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be:

Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X.
(2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award.

(3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct."

This Tribunal has been tasked with determination of just compensation.

The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller, KSRTC v. Mahadeva Shetty and Another,
(2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15):

sentences.text: Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance.
The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just.
What would be "just" compensation is a vexed question.
There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb.
Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations.
It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any.
Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration.

Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal,
the determination has to be rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims, wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..."

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial;
(iii) other material loss.

So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life."

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In view of Section 166(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act and the settled law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Malati Sardar vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd. (Civil Appeal No.
10/2016 arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 27243 of 2015)
, it is well established that a claim petition can be instituted at a place where the insurance company carries on its business.
(c) It is evident from the record that the FIR was registered on the basis of the statement of the injured himself and is duly supported by the medico-legal report as well as GD Entry No.34.
Pursuant thereto, investigation was conducted in the usual course including preparation of site plan, mechanical inspection of the offending vehicle, issuance of notice under Section 133 of the Motor Vehicles Act to the driver- cum-owner and recording of statements of witnesses under Section 161 Cr.P.C.
Thus, the contemporaneous criminal record and medical evidence form a consistent chain showing that the accident had in fact taken place and that the claimant sustained injuries therein.
Hence, there remains no doubt regarding occurrence of accident or factum of injuries.
Moreover, the FIR records presence of other persons at the spot who assisted the injured and the registration number could also have been collectively noticed.
In any case, identity of the offending vehicle does not rest solely on PW-1, as the same stands corroborated by investigation including notice under Section 133 MV Act, mechanical inspection and filing of charge-sheet.
In MACT proceedings, delay in lodging FIR is not fatal when medical exigency intervenes and the accident is otherwise supported by medical and criminal record.
Mere delay, by itself, does not discredit the claimant.
(g) PW-1 admitted that he himself did not possess a driving licence.
However, he was not driving the motorcycle and was only a pillion rider.
Even otherwise, absence of driving licence on the part of victim is not determinative of negligence unless causal connection is established, which is absent in the present case.
The subsequent medical record clearly mentions road traffic accident and therefore this objection is without merit.
(i) Minor lapses such as inability to recall motorcycle number, non-seizure of motorcycle or absence of street lighting are peripheral circumstances and do not strike at the core issue, particularly when PW-1 consistently maintained that the offending vehicle struck from behind.
Non-examination of Janmajay is also not fatal, as the injured himself has testified and his version is corroborated by criminal record.
(j) It is also relevant that when a stationary or slow-moving vehicle is hit from behind, primary responsibility lies upon the vehicle coming from the rear, which is expected to maintain safe distance and proper control.
(n) It is settled that filing of charge sheet itself is a significant step towards the inference of negligence on the part of driver of the offending vehicle.

It is also settled that proceedings under the Motor Vehicles Act are different from regular civil suits and are not strictly governed by the technical rules of the Indian Evidence Act.
